title: Jeremiah 31:31–37
context: The LORD promises a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah (31:31), not like the covenant made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt, which they broke although he was a husband to them (31:32). He will put his law in their inward parts and write it in their heart, be their God and they his people (31:33); they will no longer need to teach one another “Know the LORD,” for all will know him, from the least to the greatest, because he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (31:34). The New Testament takes up this promise: Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes it in full and Hebrews 10:16–17 in part, and Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25, and 2 Corinthians 3:6 speak of the new covenant. Both traditions read the promise as fulfilled in Christ. Their difference over how the law is written on hearts and who belongs to the covenant is already treated at Hebrews 8:10 and Hebrews 8:11, and the related question of the new heart at Deuteronomy 10:16 (with Deuteronomy 30:6); those discussions are not restated here. Readers also differ on how the promise to Israel and Judah relates to the church and to the future of Israel; those views run across both traditions. In 31:35–37 the LORD, who gives the sun by day and the moon and stars by night and stirs up the sea, declares that only if these ordinances depart, or if heaven can be measured and the earth’s foundations searched out, will Israel’s offspring cease or be cast off. The point is the faithfulness of the Creator’s pledge, expressed in the language of the created order; the passage is not a science text and is not used to settle questions about cosmology (compare 33:20–26, where the same kind of pledge is applied to David and the Levites).

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah,
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the days come … that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah.” Arminian readers see God’s gracious initiative to establish a better covenant, fulfilled in Christ (compare Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8), into which people enter by faith, and they note that both houses are again included.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same promise as God’s sovereign resolve to do what the people could not, fulfilled in Christ, who mediates the new covenant (compare Hebrews 8:6). Shared ground: both traditions read the new covenant as fulfilled in Christ and enjoyed by his people, though readers in both differ on how it relates to the future of Israel.

verses.text: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The new covenant is “not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers … which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them.” Arminian readers see the failure of the old covenant people as real covenant-breaking, which shows that covenant faithfulness matters and that God’s love can be spurned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast as central: the old covenant was broken, but the new covenant will not be, because God himself secures it (compare Hebrews 8:9). Shared ground: both traditions read “I was a husband to them” as God’s faithful love, and both locate the failure in the people rather than in the LORD.

verses.text: “But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says the LORD: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart.” Arminian readers see the Spirit’s inward renewal enabling obedience, a renewal received and continued by faith. The site’s discussion at Hebrews 8:10 treats the two readings of this promise, and the new heart at Deuteronomy 10:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God sovereignly writing his law on the hearts of all who belong to the new covenant, so that obedience flows from a renewed nature. The site’s discussion at Hebrews 8:10 treats this. Shared ground: both traditions see the new covenant writing God’s law on hearts, and both hear the covenant formula renewed (compare 30:22).

verses.text: They will no longer each teach his neighbor, and every man teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD;’ for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest,” says the LORD, “for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises that “they will all know me, from their least to their greatest … for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.” Arminian readers see personal knowledge of God opened to all in the new covenant, grounded in full forgiveness for all who enter it by faith. The site’s discussion at Hebrews 8:11 treats this.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see all genuine new covenant members actually knowing God, which shapes their view of who belongs to it, and they see forgiveness secured by Christ’s sacrifice. The site’s discussion at Hebrews 8:11 treats this. Shared ground: both traditions see a new intimacy with God and complete forgiveness as the heart of the promise.

verses.text: The LORD, who gives the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, who stirs up the sea, so that its waves roar— the LORD of Armies is his name, says:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD describes himself as the one who gives the sun by day and the moon and stars by night and stirs up the sea, “the LORD of Armies is his name.” Arminian readers see the Creator’s faithfulness displayed in the regular order of creation, which grounds confidence in his promises to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same order as the work of the sovereign Creator who governs all things, so his covenant word is as reliable as the sunrise. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as doxology about the Creator, not as a science text, and both hear the name “LORD of Armies” as underlining his power to keep what he promises.

verses.text: “If these ordinances depart from before me,” says the LORD, “then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: “If these ordinances depart from before me … then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.” Arminian readers see a solemn pledge of God’s faithfulness to Israel, and they note that readers in their tradition differ over how the pledge applies to ethnic Israel and to the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same pledge as God’s unbreakable commitment to his covenant people, and readers in this tradition likewise differ over its application to Israel and the church (compare Romans 11:1–2, 29). Shared ground: both traditions read the comparison with the fixed order as an image of certainty, not a statement about cosmology.

verses.text: The LORD says: “If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, then I will also cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, then I will also cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done.” Arminian readers see that God’s faithfulness outlasts Israel’s sins, and they read the image as poetic certainty rather than a claim about scientific measurement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s refusal to cast off his people “for all that they have done” as grace that rests on his promise, not their performance. Shared ground: both traditions read the immeasurable heavens as a figure for impossibility, and the site’s discussion at Romans 11:29 treats the related question of God’s faithfulness to Israel’s calling.
